solution:
Velocity.
The internal movements of the earth are classified on the basis of their velocity, their direction and the landforms they produce. It is on the basis of velocity that they are divided into slow movements, which go on continuously and build mountains and continents, and sudden movements, which occur as events such as earthquakes and volcanoes. So a movement is called slow or sudden according to its velocity.

Tension.
When waves move away from each other, the rocks lying between them are pulled in opposite directions and tension is created in the earth's crust. As this tension increases, fractures develop in the rocks and faults are formed. Waves moving towards each other create compression, which is the opposite case.

Tension.
A rift valley is formed when horizontal movements act in opposite directions and create tension in the rocks of the earth's crust. When the tension increases, two fractures develop side by side and the land lying between them subsides; this deep subsided part is the rift valley, and both its slopes are steep. Compression pushes the rocks together and forms folds, and weathering only wears the rocks down, so neither of them can produce a rift valley.

The Himalayas.
The Himalayas, the Aravalis, the Rockies, the Andes and the Alps are the major fold mountains of the world. They were formed when energy waves and pressure working towards each other in the horizontal direction folded the layers of soft rocks, so that the surface of the earth was uplifted.
[Note: the chapter does not state how the Satpudas and the Western Ghats were formed; about the Sahyadri it only says that it is made of layers of lava deposited by volcanic eruption.]

Continent-building.
Continent-building (epeirogenic) movements are slow movements that occur towards the centre of the earth or from the earth's centre towards the crust. Because of them a vast part of the earth's crust is uplifted or subsides. When such a large part is uplifted above the mean sea level, continents are formed, and extensive plateaus can also be formed by the same movements.

The forward and backward movement was the work of the primary waves of the earthquake. Primary or P waves are the first waves to reach the earth's surface after the energy is released in the earth's interior, and they travel at a very fast speed from the focus in a radial direction. The particles of rock lying in their way move to and fro in the direction in which the wave is travelling, and that is why these are also called forward-backward waves; the buildings standing on the surface therefore move back and forth. The secondary waves reached the buildings next and shook them up and down, and these are more destructive than the primary waves; after them came the surface waves, which are highly destructive. The buildings could not bear this shaking and collapsed. The foothills of the Himalayas were affected because this mountainous zone of Asia lies in an earthquake-prone belt, as fig 2.18 shows.

The two plateaus were formed by two entirely different internal processes. The Meghalaya Plateau was formed by faulting. Horizontal movements acting in opposite directions created tension in the rocks of the crust; fractures, that is faults, developed, and the part of the crust lying between two parallel faults was lifted up so that it looked like a block. Such a landform has a flat top and steep slopes, and the Black Forest mountains of Europe were formed in the same way. The Deccan Plateau, on the other hand, was formed by a fissure-type volcanic eruption. The magma came out not from a single vent but from many cracks, and the molten material spread on both sides of the fissures; this spreading lava built a volcanic plateau. So one is the result of faulting in the crust and the other of volcanic eruption, and that is why there is a difference in their formation.

The earth's crust is made up of plates, and the oceans and continents lie spread over these plates. Depending on the compression and tension created in the interior of the earth, the plates keep moving in various directions, so their boundaries are the most disturbed parts of the crust. At some boundaries a part of the plate slides under the crust and material is lost there; such boundaries are called plate consuming (subduction) boundaries. At other boundaries new material comes up on to the earth's crust, and these are called plate creating (constructive) boundaries. Both these processes go on continuously, so the hot material of the interior finds its way out to the surface mainly along the plate boundaries. That is why fig 2.18 shows most of the volcanoes, and the earthquake zones as well, lying along the boundaries of the plates.

Barren Island is taking the shape of a cone because its eruptions are of the central type. In a central-type eruption the molten magma comes out through a single pipe-like vent, and the material thrown out spreads around the mouth of that vent. Dust, smoke, mud and some lava have been coming out of Barren Island since it started erupting, and each time this material settles around the same mouth. As layer piles upon layer, the heap stays highest at the vent and slopes away on all sides, so a cone-shaped mountain slowly takes form. Mt. Fujiyama in Japan and Mt. Kilimanjaro in Tanzania are the chapter's examples of such central-type volcanoes and conical mountains.
[Note: the chapter does not itself state that Barren Island is a central-type volcano; this has been worked out from the way it describes the formation of conical volcanic mountains.]

A volcanic eruption is one of the causes of earthquakes listed in the chapter. Because of the movements occurring in the interior of the earth, tremendous tension is created in the earth's crust, and when this tension goes beyond limits the energy is released in the form of waves, which makes the earth's surface tremble. A volcanic eruption is exactly such a violent release, for in it hot solid, liquid and gaseous materials are thrown out of the mantle on to the surface of the earth. This forces the rocks of the crust to give way and sends energy waves out through them, and these waves shake the ground around. So an eruption can set off an earthquake, and when the eruption occurs below an ocean floor it can even generate tsunamis.

This is a sudden movement - an earthquake. The chapter counts the generating of tsunamis among the effects of earthquakes: when an earthquake occurs, tsunamis are generated in the oceans, and these waves can cause great loss of life and property in the coastal areas. The chapter also notes that tsunamis are sometimes generated by volcanic eruptions occurring below ocean floors, which is a sudden movement of the same kind.

This is a slow movement - a mountain-building (orogenic) movement. Energy is transferred from the interior of the earth, and these energy waves and the pressure work towards each other in the horizontal direction. This compression bends the layers of the soft rocks into folds; when the pressure is very high the folds become large and complex, the surface of the earth is uplifted, and fold mountains such as the Himalayas are formed.

This is a sudden movement - a volcanic eruption. Hot solid, liquid and gaseous materials are thrown out from the mantle of the earth on to its surface, and along with them come ash, water vapour and various poisonous and inflammable gases. The molten magma is called lava once it comes out on the surface.

This is a slow movement - a mountain-building (orogenic) movement working through faulting. Horizontal movements acting in opposite directions create tension in the rocks of the earth's crust; as the tension increases, fractures called faults develop and the continuity of the rock layers is broken. Where two fractures develop side by side, the land lying between them subsides, and this deep subsided part is the rift valley, with steep slopes on both sides. The rift valley of the river Narmada in India, the Great Rift Valley of Africa and the Rhine river rift valley of Europe are examples.

The correct chronological order is (c), (b), (d), (e), (a).

1. (c) Due to the movements in the mantle, compression goes on increasing. The movements in the earth's interior come first, and they slowly build up pressure in the crust above.
2. (b) The plates suddenly move. The earth's crust is made up of plates, and when the pressure crosses the limit the rocks can bear, the plates move, collide, or slide one below the other.
3. (d) Along the weak points (faultlines) rocks break apart. The rocks give way first at their weakest places, where fractures already exist.
4. (e) Stored energy is released in the form of seismic waves. The energy stored up in the strained rocks is set free at the focus the moment they break, and it spreads out in all directions as waves.
5. (a) The earth's surface vibrates. The waves reach the surface, first at the epicentre and then in the areas further away, and the ground trembles. This trembling is the earthquake.

| Point of difference | Block Mountain | Fold Mountain |
|---|---|---|

| How the landform comes up | The part of the earth's crust lying between two parallel faults is lifted up, and it looks like a block. | The large-scale folding uplifts the surface of the earth itself. |
| Shape | The hilltops are flat, in the early stages they have no peaks, and the slopes are steep. | The chapter does not state this. |
| Examples | The Black Forest mountains in Europe; the Meghalaya Plateau of India. | The Himalayas, the Aravalis, the Rockies, the Andes and the Alps. |

[Note: the chapter does not describe the shape of the tops or the slopes of fold mountains, though it does describe them for block mountains.]

|---|---|---|

| Speed | They travel at a very fast speed from the focus in a radial direction. | Their velocity is lesser than that of the P waves. |
| Movement of the particles | The particles in the rock move to and fro in the direction of the waves, so these are also called forward-backward waves. | The particles lying in the way of these waves move up and down. |
| Medium through which they travel | They can travel through all the three states - solid, liquid and gaseous - but their direction gets changed while travelling through a liquid medium. | They can travel only through a solid medium and get absorbed as they enter a liquid medium. |

| Point of difference | Earthquake | Volcano |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | 'Earth' means the ground and 'quake' means trembling; an earthquake is the trembling movement of the earth's crust. | A volcano is the process in which hot solid, liquid and gaseous materials are thrown out from the mantle of the earth on to its surface. |
| How it happens | The movements in the interior create tremendous tension in the crust; when the tension goes beyond limits, the energy is released at the focus in the form of waves. | Ash, water vapour, poisonous and inflammable gases and hot molten magma are thrown out, either through a single pipe-like vent or through many cracks; the magma is called lava once it is on the surface. |
| Types | The energy travels as three types of seismic waves - primary, secondary and surface waves. | On the basis of the type of eruption there are central or conical and fissure-type volcanoes; on the basis of periodicity there are active, dormant and extinct volcanoes. |
| Measurement | The magnitude is measured by the Richter scale, and the waves are recorded by a seismogram. | The chapter does not state this. |
| Landforms produced | Cracks and fractures develop on the ground, some areas get uplifted and some subside. | Conical volcanic mountains and volcanic plateaus are formed, new land may be created, and lakes form in the craters of dead volcanoes. |
| Effects | Buildings collapse with loss of life and property, landslides occur, tsunamis are generated in oceans, and transport and communication break down. | There is loss of life and property, tsunamis may be generated by eruptions below ocean floors, dust and gases upset the environment, but the land becomes fertile from volcanic ash and many minerals are found near the surface because of lava. |

[Note: the chapter gives no instrument or scale for measuring a volcanic eruption, though it gives the Richter scale and the seismogram for earthquakes.]

Because of the movements occurring in the interior of the earth, tremendous tension is created in the earth's crust, and when this tension goes beyond limits the energy is released in the form of waves; this trembling of the earth's crust is an earthquake. The chapter gives the following causes for it. The plates of which the crust is made keep moving, for they shift in various directions according to the compression and tension created inside the earth. The plates collide with one another, and sometimes one plate slides below another. Fractures form in the rock layers because of the tension in the interior, and the rocks break apart along these weak lines. Volcanic eruptions are also a cause of earthquakes. In every case the energy set free at the focus spreads out as seismic waves and makes the surface vibrate.

The major fold mountains of the world have been formed by slow movements, namely the mountain-building or orogenic movements working in the horizontal direction. Energy is transferred from the interior of the earth, and these energy waves and the pressure work towards each other, so compression is created in the crust. Because of this compression the layers of the soft rocks bend and folds are formed in them. If the pressure is very high, large-scale folds are formed and their complexity increases. As a result the surface of the earth gets uplifted and fold mountains are formed. The Himalayas, the Aravalis, the Rockies, the Andes and the Alps have all been formed in this way.

The magnitude of an earthquake shows how much energy has been released at its focus, and it is measured on the Richter scale from the graph that a seismogram draws. The greater the magnitude, the greater is the energy that travels outward as seismic waves, and the more violently the ground and the houses standing on it are shaken. The primary waves make the houses move back and forth, the secondary waves shake them up and down and are more destructive, and the surface waves that follow are highly destructive. A tremor of small magnitude may only crack the walls, but when the magnitude is high the houses cannot bear the shaking and collapse. This can be understood from the activity at the beginning of the chapter, where a slight push hardly disturbs the pile of notebooks but a hard push brings the whole structure down. The earthquake of 7.9 magnitude described in the news item shook the ground so strongly that buildings came down and nearly 1500 people were killed.

An earthquake changes the earth's surface in many ways. Cracks and fractures develop on the ground, and landslides are caused which make rocks slide down. Sometimes the groundwater changes its course, so that wells may suddenly get water or may dry up. Some areas get uplifted while others subside; tsunamis are generated in the oceans, and in snow-covered areas avalanches may occur. Human life is affected just as badly, for buildings collapse and there is loss of life and property. Transportation routes get disrupted and the communication system collapses, so help is hard to reach the affected people. The tsunami waves that reach the shore can cause great loss of life and property in the coastal areas.

[Textbook misprint: describing secondary waves the chapter says the particles "move up and down in the direction of energy transfer", which contradicts itself — up-and-down motion is at right angles to the direction in which the wave carries its energy, not along it. The rest of the chapter's account is consistent with the standard one (S waves arrive after P waves, are slower, travel only through solids, are absorbed by liquids, and shake buildings up and down), so the answer below keeps everything the chapter says except that one clause.]

When the tension is released at the focus, the energy travels in all directions and comes towards the earth's surface in the form of waves. These seismic waves are of three types.

(1) Primary or 'P' waves: These are the first ones to reach the surface of the earth after the energy is emitted in the earth's interior. They travel at a very fast speed from the focus in a radial direction. The particles of rock lying in their way move to and fro in the direction of the waves, and so they are also called forward-backward waves. They can travel through all the three states - solid, liquid and gaseous - but their direction gets changed while they travel through a liquid medium. It is because of them that buildings on the surface move back and forth.

(2) Secondary or 'S' waves: These reach the earth's surface after the primary waves, and they too scatter in all directions from the focus. Their velocity is lesser than that of the P waves. The particles lying in their way move up and down. These waves can travel only through a solid medium and get absorbed as they enter a liquid medium. Buildings on the surface move up and down because of them, and they are more destructive than the P waves.

(3) Surface or 'L' waves: These are generated after the main P and S waves reach the epicentre. They travel along the crust, in the direction of the circumference of the earth. They are highly destructive.

[Textbook misprint: the chapter contradicts itself about Barren Island. Its list of volcano types gives Barren Island as an example of a DORMANT volcano, but the box on printed page 19 calls it "India's only active volcano", noting it was dormant for a long time and started erupting in February 2017. Both statements are reproduced below so the reader can see the conflict; on the book's own later evidence Barren Island is active.]

According to the periodicity of their eruptions, three types of volcanoes can be identified.

(1) Active volcanoes: those whose eruptions are regular even in the present times. For example, Mt. Fujiyama in Japan and Mt. Stromboli in the Mediterranean Sea.

(2) Dormant volcanoes: those which have not erupted since long, but may become active suddenly. For example, Mt. Vesuvius in Italy, Mt. Katmai in Alaska and Barren Island in India.

(3) Extinct volcanoes: those which have not erupted in the past since long and are not likely to erupt in the future. For example, Mt. Kilimanjaro in Tanzania.

The chapter itself shows how a dormant volcano can turn active: it says that Barren Island, which lies on the Andaman and Nicobar archipelago and is given above as an example of a dormant volcano, was dormant for a long time but started erupting in February 2017, and it calls it India's only active volcano.

Draw the diagram as a section, that is a side view, of a part of the earth, and label every part neatly.

1. Draw a rectangle to show a block of the earth. Draw a straight horizontal line across the top of it and label it 'Earth's surface'.

2. Mark a small dark point well inside the block, at a good depth below the surface, and label it 'Focus'. This is the place where the tension mounts up and the energy is released.

3. From the focus draw a straight vertical dotted line upwards till it meets the surface line. Mark that meeting point clearly and label it 'Epicentre'. The line must be vertical, because the epicentre is the nearest place on the earth's surface from the focus and lies perpendicular to it; it is the place that experiences the first tremor.

4. From the focus draw arcs, or arrows with arrowheads, spreading outwards in all directions like the ripples made by a stone dropped in water. Label the outer set 'Primary waves', because they travel fastest and reach the surface first, and label the set just behind them 'Secondary waves', because they reach the surface after the primary waves. The arrowheads show that both these waves move outward from the focus in a radial direction.

5. From the epicentre draw waves running to the left and to the right along the surface line itself, and label them 'Surface waves'. They are drawn along the surface because they are generated after the main primary and secondary waves reach the epicentre, and they travel along the crust in the direction of the circumference of the earth.

6. Write the title 'Types of seismic waves' below the figure, and keep every label outside the diagram, joined to its part by a thin pointing line.

Mark each place on the outline map of the world with a small triangle or a dot, write its name beside it, and show the sign you have used in an index in one corner of the map.

(a) Mt. Kilimanjaro - in Tanzania, in the eastern part of Africa. In fig 2.18 it is shown in eastern Africa, close to the boundary of the Somali Plate.

(b) Mid-Atlantic Earthquake zone - in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. In fig 2.18 an earthquake zone runs roughly from north to south down the centre of the Atlantic Ocean, between North and South America on the west and Europe and Africa on the east, following a plate creating (constructive) boundary. Show it as a long belt down the middle of the ocean, not as a single point.

(c) Mt. Fuji - in Japan, on the chain of islands lying off the eastern coast of Asia, where fig 2.18 shows the boundary between the Eurasian Plate and the Pacific Plate. The chapter calls it Mt. Fujiyama and gives it as an example both of an active volcano and of a central-type conical volcano.

(d) Krakatoa - on the belt of islands of south-east Asia, between the mainland of Asia and Australia and close to the equator, along the boundary between the Eurasian Plate and the Indo-Australian Plate, as shown in fig 2.18.

(e) Mt. Vesuvius - in Italy, in southern Europe, near the Mediterranean Sea. The chapter gives it as an example of a dormant volcano.

[Note: the chapter does not name the country in which Krakatoa lies, and it does not use the name 'Mid-Atlantic Earthquake zone' anywhere in its text; both of these have been located only from the world map in fig 2.18.]
